Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette:
The event that fractured Amir’s world happened three years ago, on a late summer evening. He had just finished a rehearsal for a community theatre production and was walking home through the park when he heard a child crying. It was not an unusual sound, but something in the pitch made him stop. He turned toward the noise and saw a group of people gathered near the pond; a woman was on her knees, screaming. It was his daughter, Leila. She had been struck by a car that had mounted the curb, and by the time Amir reached her, she was gone. The paramedics arrived too late, and the driver—a man who had been texting—was never charged. The district attorney cited insufficient evidence, and the case was closed in weeks.

In the months that followed, Amir found that his memories of that evening did not form a coherent story. He could see Leila’s face in perfect, photographic detail—the way her hair fell across the pavement—but he could not remember how he had gotten from the park bench to her side. The pieces were fragmented, disconnected, and each time one surfaced, it brought a wave of guilt so intense he could barely breathe. He was certain he should have done more, should have run faster, should have somehow stopped the car. He told himself that the legal system had failed them both, that the driver had faced no consequences, and that the institutions meant to protect his family had simply let them down.

These appraisals fed directly into a constant, low-grade threat that Amir could not shake. Even when friends or his therapist told him he was safe, he found it impossible to believe. He could not concentrate on scripts or rehearsals; his mind was always scanning for danger. The sound of a child crying, even on television, would send his heart racing and his thoughts spiraling back to the park. Media coverage of similar accidents became unbearable, and he began to avoid the news entirely.

To manage this pervasive threat, Amir developed a set of strategies that, over time, reshaped his life. He became a people pleaser, agreeing with whatever others wanted because disagreeing felt too risky, as if any conflict might invite catastrophe. He could not bear to be alone in his apartment—the silence amplified the guilt—so he started spending evenings at a friend’s house, often staying until late. But crowds, too, became unbearable; shopping centres and public events felt like traps, full of unpredictable sounds and movements. He began to restrict his outings to early mornings, when the streets were empty.

These strategies, however, only deepened the cycle. Avoiding crowds meant he missed auditions and rehearsals, which reinforced his sense of failure and inaction. The guilt on recall grew sharper because he felt he was no longer living a meaningful life—he was just surviving. The fragmented memories intruded more frequently when he was alone, so he avoided solitude, but the constant company exhausted him and made it harder to concentrate. Every time he heard a child cry—in a store, on a street corner, in a movie—it triggered the full cascade: the memory, the guilt, the anger at the system, and the urgent need to escape.

By the time Amir sought help, he had lost two major acting roles, stopped seeing most of his friends, and was sleeping on a cousin’s couch because his own apartment felt haunted. What frightened him most was the possibility that he would never forgive himself—that the guilt would always be there, waiting in the silence. He came to therapy because he was tired of running, and because, for the first time in three years, he wanted to believe that safety might still exist somewhere, even if he could not yet feel it.
